title: I Lubed 90 Switches So You Don't Have To (Is It Worth It?)
creator: keebsbyraf
description:
Hand lubing switches: worth it, or a waste of a weekend? I timed the whole thing.

Keyboard: Keychron Q1 Max
Switches: Gateron Milky Yellow Pro
Lube: Krytox 205g0
Switch opener + lube station: generic

Affiliate disclosure: the Amazon links in this description are affiliate links. I earn a small commission from qualifying purchases, at no extra cost to you.
Keychron Q1 Max: https://amzn.to/4cP1xYr
Krytox 205g0: https://amzn.to/3Wm7rTb
Switch opener: https://amzn.to/3Qz8NkD

0:00 Intro
0:40 What I'm using
1:30 Opening switches
2:50 Lubing

Discord: discord.gg/keebsbyraf

sentences.t: So I have ninety switches here, and every single one of them needs to be opened, lubed, and closed again.
People keep telling me hand lubing is the biggest upgrade you can make to a keyboard.
And I keep saying I'm too lazy, so today I'm actually doing it, and I'm timing it.
Let's see if it's worth an entire Saturday.
Okay, first, here's what I'm working with, because I get asked this on literally every video.
The board is a Keychron Q1 Max, the switches are Gateron Milky Yellows, and the lube is Krytox two oh five.
Everything I use is linked in the description, and those Amazon links are affiliate links.
That means if you pick something up through them, I get a tiny commission and you don't pay any more.
It's honestly how I afford to keep buying keyboards I don't need, so I appreciate it.
But there's zero pressure, half of this stuff you can get cheaper secondhand on the forums.
Alright, step one, opening the switches.
This little thing is a switch opener, you push the switch in, press down, and the top pops off.
Like that.
And then you've got the top housing, the stem, the spring, and the bottom housing.
Do not lose the springs, I'm saying that now because I will lose a spring.
I'm going to do them in batches of ten so I don't go completely insane.
Okay, ten done, that took about four minutes, which means ninety is going to be like forty minutes just opening.
We're fine, it's fine.
Alright, step two, the actual lubing, which is the part everyone argues about.
You want a really thin layer, like, thinner than you think.
If you can see it shining, it's probably too much.
I'm doing the stem legs and the sides of the stem, and a little bit on the bottom housing rails.
Do not lube the legs that touch the metal contact on linears, well, okay, people do, but I don't, it gets mushy.
This brush is a size zero, which is basically a few hairs on a stick.
Dip, wipe most of it off on the side of the jar, then brush.
And the springs, I'm bag lubing those, which is where you put them in a little bag with a drop of oil and shake.
Very scientific, I know.
Okay, I'm going to speed this part up because nobody needs to watch me do this for two hours.
Two hours and eleven minutes later, and yes, I lost exactly one spring, it's somewhere in my carpet forever.
Luckily I had spares.
Alright, putting them back into the board.
Okay, the moment of truth, sound test.
Here's the stock switches on my other board first, same switch, not lubed.
Kind of scratchy, right, you can hear a little bit of that rattle on the way down.
And now the lubed ones.
Okay, yeah, I hate to say it, but they were right.
It's deeper, it's smoother, there's no scratch at all, it just kind of thocks.
And typing on it, the feel is the bigger difference, it just glides.
So is it worth it, honestly, if you have a free weekend and a podcast queued up, yes.
If you hate fiddly work, buy switches that come factory lubed and save yourself the pain.
The Milky Yellow Pros are already decent out of the box, so the jump was smaller than it would be on cheap switches.
Final time, three hours and two minutes for ninety switches, including the spring hunt.
Let me know if you want me to try the same thing with tactiles, because those are way harder to get right.
And if you've got a tip for not losing springs, please, I'm begging you, put it in the comments.
Okay, that's it, I'm going to go type something very long and very pointless, see you.
